name: force_the_lock
title: Force the Lock
description: Attempt to force a lock, quietly or otherwise. Reference specimen: exercises every key the custom-tool format understands. Copy it to Tools/force-the-lock.tool.json in any document store, then cut it down to what you actually need — every key here except name, description and outcomes is optional. `title` is what Pascal announces and what the popup lists; omit it and the name is title-cased instead, as CUSTOM_TOOL_SPEC_DICE.json does. The model never sees it — it calls the tool by `name`.

bonus.description: Skill bonus added to the score. Demonstrates: a number parameter, bounds, and a $param reference used as the roll's offset. Note the knock-on: at the default 0 the score tops out at exactly the ceiling, so the first outcome (> 100) only fires when a bonus is supplied — which is rather the point of a bonus. Run-time values are clamped into 0-10 before the roll ever sees them.

ceiling.description: Top of the difficulty scale. Demonstrates: a $param reference used as the roll's multiplier, so the 0-1 draw is scaled into 0-ceiling.

attempts.description: How many times you try. Demonstrates: an integer parameter (run-time values are rounded) and {{params.attempts}} in a message.

label.description: What you are forcing. Demonstrates: a string parameter. Strings cannot be referenced by $param — only numbers and integers can.

loudly.description: Whether you are past caring about the noise. Demonstrates: a boolean parameter. Booleans cannot be referenced by $param either.

llm.prompt: A lockpicking attempt on {{params.label}} scored {{value}} against a ceiling of {{params.ceiling}} (raw draw {{roll}}). In one word, YES or NO: was it elegant? — Demonstrates the llm consult: this prompt is rendered with the same placeholders a message takes ({{llm}} excepted — the oracle cannot quote an answer it has not yet given) and posed to the instance's cheap utility model once per run, after the roll and before the outcome table.
llm.errorMessage: The oracle of locks is not answering today. (Demonstrates errorMessage: the consult's output when the call fails — the author's words, never the provider's. The technical failure reason goes to the roll record and the logs, not the fiction.)

outcomes.message: The pick shears off in {{params.label}}. Demonstrates the `roll` subject: this tests the RAW 0-1 draw ({{roll}}), not the scaled score ({{value}}), so it means the same thing however the ceiling and bonus move the value about — which is a thing `value` alone cannot express. It sits first because a draw that low would otherwise be swallowed by the lt:5 band below.

{{params.label}} does not so much open as capitulate. The score was {{value}} — past the ceiling of {{params.ceiling}} entirely, which is what a bonus of {{params.bonus}} will do for a person. (Raw draw: {{roll}}.) Demonstrates a $param operand: the test is against a number the caller supplied, not one fixed here. This is how an opposed check is written.

{{params.label}} opens to the skeleton key before the score of {{value}} is properly consulted. Demonstrates the `metadata` subject: this tests the INVOKING character's metadata.json fact sheet (hasSkeletonKey = {{metadata.hasSkeletonKey}}), whose keys this file never declares — so the loader checks only the comparator's shape. A character without the key is not an error: the test simply fails, soft, and the roll falls through to the rows below. eq/neq address strings and booleans; ordering comparators need the sheet to hold a number, as the nerve row demonstrates further down.

{{llm}} — Demonstrates the consult's failure path, and where {{llm}} gets its words when the oracle is silent: the answer BECOMES the llm block's errorMessage, ok goes false, and the run itself never errors. A table that keeps an oracle should decide what silence means; an ok:false row like this is one way, trusting the catch-all is the other.

"{{llm}}," pronounces the oracle, and {{params.label}} concedes the point at {{value}}. Demonstrates the `llm` subject: eq/neq compare the trimmed answer without regard to case (a trailing full stop is forgiven — a model that says "yes." has still said yes), ordering comparators apply when the answer reads as a number and otherwise decline the row fail-soft, and `ok` — the one non-comparator key — tests whether the consult produced an answer at all.

{{params.label}} gives up at {{value}}, and so does any pretence of discretion — that noise was heard three streets over. Demonstrates the `params` subject ANDed with a value band: score 70-100 AND loudly=true. It must sit BEFORE the quiet band below, which it would otherwise never outrank.
{{params.label}} clicks open on attempt {{params.attempts}}. Score {{value}}. Demonstrates an AND band: gte and lte in one object mean 70 <= value <= 100. There is no OR — order the table instead.
The tumblers settle on exactly {{value}}, which you choose to find significant. Demonstrates the eq comparator.
{{params.label}} shifts, then thinks better of it. Score {{value}}. Demonstrates neq composed with a band — 40 to 50, but never 42, which the outcome above already claimed.

A dreadful draw — {{value}} — salvaged by sheer nerve ({{metadata.nerve}} of a possible 10). Demonstrates an ORDERING comparator on metadata: gte needs a number on both sides, and since the sheet cannot be known at load time the check waits for the roll — a character whose nerve is absent, a string, or a list simply does not match, fail-soft, no error, and the draw falls through to the failures below. And {{metadata.limerick}}, a key this character surely lacks, stays exactly as written — metadata placeholders for missing keys render verbatim, like any unknown placeholder.

The safe declines to notice you at all. Score {{value}}. Demonstrates eq against a STRING parameter: ordering comparators (gt/gte/lt/lte) need numbers on both sides, but eq and neq will address a string or a boolean. A mismatch — eq: 5 against a string parameter — is rejected when the file loads rather than quietly never firing.

Whatever {{params.label}} is, it is door-shaped enough to lean on, and it does not move. Score {{value}}. Demonstrates contains against a STRING parameter: the test holds when the parameter's text holds the substring, case-sensitively; ncontains is its complement, and an empty substring is rejected at load (everything contains ""). The substring may itself be a { "$param": "..." } reference to another string parameter, so one input can be sought inside another. metadata and llm subjects take contains too — fail-soft on a key that is not a string, and, on the consult's answer, trimmed and case-insensitive like eq there.
Something inside {{params.label}} snaps, and it was not the lock. Score {{value}}. Demonstrates the lt comparator.
{{params.label}} holds, smugly. Score {{value}}. Demonstrates lte, and why order matters: this must sit AFTER lt:5, or lt:5 could never be reached.

{{params.label}} is giving way — slowly, and (loudly: {{params.loudly}}) not discreetly. Score {{value}} from a raw draw of {{roll}}. This is the mandatory catch-all: the LAST outcome must be `true`, and no earlier one may be, so every roll lands somewhere and nothing below is unreachable.
